description: NASA plans to put a 100 kWe fission reactor on the lunar surface by 2030. Its shield casts a protective “shadow,” and step outside that cone and crew radiation dose jumps 10×. Current designs assume short Artemis stays. A permanent base breaks those assumptions, and no public tool shows the tradeoff.
summary:
Shadowline is a browser game about one mission design question: how close can a 100 kWe fission reactor sit to astronauts on the Moon? Players lay out a lunar south pole base on real NASA LOLA terrain of the Shackleton rim: a reactor with a directional shadow shield, a crew habitat, and a daily moonwalk route to a science site. Every choice trades power delivered, cable mass and regolith moved against crew radiation dose, judged against the NASA-STD-3001 limit of 20 mSv per mission year for nuclear sources.

Two levels use the same layout. For a 33-day Artemis sortie, the published 1 km layout gives 5.3 mSv and passes. For a 365-day permanent outpost, the same layout gives 59 mSv, 2.9 times the limit, and the player has to redesign it using distance, regolith berms, terrain masking, or a route that stays inside the shield's shadow.

It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting students make real engineering decisions with limited resources and see how each one changes mission success. Every constant in the model is listed in the game with its source and how far to trust it.
details:
What it does

Shadowline puts the player in charge of siting a fission surface power reactor at the lunar south pole. On a map built from NASA LOLA elevation data (Site04 on the Shackleton rim, 5 m/px source data resampled to 40 m/px), the player drags the reactor and habitat, adds waypoints to the crew's daily EVA route to a fixed science site, and builds regolith berms. A live dose map and a white 20 mSv contour show where crews can and cannot spend time. A side panel reports four budgets: power delivered, cable mass, regolith moved, and crew dose against NASA limits.

How it works

The dose model is deliberately simple. It is calibrated to published anchor values instead of a transport calculation.

Inside the 36 degree shield shadow: 5 rem/yr at 1 km, scaled by the inverse square of distance.

Outside the shadow: 50 rem/yr at 1 km, scaled the same way.

Regolith on the line of sight (terrain or a berm) attenuates dose exponentially. The coefficient is contested in the literature, so the game exposes it as a slider.

Mission dose is the sum of dose rate times hours at each location. The habitat interior applies a shielding factor.

Cable mass is 73 kg per km of reactor-to-habitat distance.

Reactor dose (limit 20 mSv per mission year), the 600 mSv career limit and natural background are shown as three separate budgets and are never mixed.

The two levels

Level 1, Artemis Sortie, 33 days: the published 1 km layout gives 5.3 mSv, within the limit.

Level 2, Permanent Outpost, 365 days: the same layout gives 59 mSv, 2.9 times the limit. The player must redesign using alignment inside the shadow, distance, berms or terrain masking. Each option costs cable mass, excavation, or freedom of layout.

Why it matters

Published fission surface power designs assume short Artemis stays. A permanent base removes that operational margin, and we found no public tool that lets a student see the trade-off. Shadowline turns it into something a non-engineer can explore in a few minutes, with plain-language explanations of why a layout passes or fails. The game never calls a layout "safe". It says "within NASA-STD-3001 limits under these assumptions".

How we kept it honest

All 50 constants are listed in an in-game Assumptions drawer with their source and a trust level (published value, modeling assumption, or game design choice). The repository includes a verification suite of 94 automated tests that check the model against the published anchors, the inverse-square law, and an independent unshielded benchmark (reproduced within 0.3%). Known limitations are documented in the README: line of sight only (no neutron scatter or skyshine, so berms look more effective than they would be), a point source, uniform regolith, and 40 m terrain cells. It is a teaching model, not a radiation protection assessment.

Tools

TypeScript, React, Vite, HTML canvas and Vitest. Terrain preprocessing in Python with NumPy and rasterio. The built game is a static site with the terrain embedded, so it runs in a browser with no server.

Use of SI

The game's source code, tests, README and the demo slides were generated with a large language model (Anthropic's Claude) under the team's direction. This is acknowledged in the repository README and on every slide. No SI-generated images, audio or video are used. All images are screenshots of the running game.
